item.title: Blue crab
item.description: Atlantic swimming crab, Callinectes sapidus, from the Chesapeake Bay to the Gulf of Mexico. Sweet, briny, finely flaked white meat sold live, steamed whole, or picked and graded by the part of the body it comes from.

item.title: Chesapeake seafood seasoning
item.description: A homemade Old Bay-style blend: celery seed and bay leaf ground fresh, sweet paprika, black pepper, dry mustard, cayenne, and a small amount of warm spice (allspice, clove, mace, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon), cut with fine sea salt. The celery seed and bay carry it; the warm spices sit underneath.

item.title: Maryland crab cakes
item.description: Jumbo lump blue crab held together by the minimum binder that will hold it: one egg, a spoon of mayonnaise, dijon, Worcestershire, Chesapeake seasoning, and a handful of crushed saltines. Chilled to set, then seared hard in butter and oil so the outside goes deep golden while the inside stays loose, sweet, and almost all crab.

item.title: Roasted butternut squash salad with radicchio, pecans, and balsamic
item.description: Hard-roasted butternut cubes, dressed hot so they drink the vinaigrette, laid over radicchio and arugula with salted toasted pecans, crisped sage, and shaved parmigiano. Sweetness comes only from the caramelized squash and the balsamic; bitter leaves, a red wine vinegar spine, and a salty umami finish keep it a savory side rather than a dessert on a plate.

item.title: Tartar sauce
item.description: Mayonnaise sharpened with minced cornichons, capers, shallot, lemon zest and juice, dill, and a little of the pickle brine. A cold, briny, high-acid sauce built to cut fried and seared seafood.

item.title: Vinegar coleslaw
item.description: Finely shredded green cabbage and carrot, salted briefly to pull out surface water, then dressed with cider vinegar, a little sugar, oil, dijon, and celery seed. Crunchy, sharp, and mayonnaise-free, so it cuts rich seafood and fried food instead of adding to it.

item.title: Nuoc cham bun cha (Hanoi-style warm dipping broth)
item.description: The Hanoi version of nuoc cham, served warm in a deep bowl as a thin, light broth rather than a dip. Fish sauce, rice vinegar, and sugar are dissolved in a generous volume of hot water, then loaded with quick-pickled green papaya and carrot, raw garlic, and chili. Grilled pork and patties go straight into the bowl, and diners dip rice vermicelli and herbs through it.

item.title: Nuoc cham chay (vegan dipping sauce)
item.description: The Buddhist temple-kitchen nuoc cham, built without fish. Light soy sauce and a strong dried-shiitake soaking liquid stand in for the fish sauce, fresh coconut water gives the gentle sweetness and body southern cooks use in place of plain water, and lime, garlic, and chili finish it exactly like the original.

item.title: Nuoc mam gung (ginger fish sauce)
item.description: The ginger-heavy nuoc cham served with poached chicken, boiled duck, and steamed fish. Fresh ginger is pounded with sugar in a mortar until it weeps juice, then loosened with fish sauce, lime, and a little water. Thicker, hotter on the palate, and less diluted than everyday nuoc cham, so it clings to plain poached meat that has no seasoning of its own.

item.title: Nuoc mam me (tamarind fish sauce)
item.description: The southern Vietnamese sweet-sour dip for crab, snails, grilled shrimp, and fried fish. Tamarind pulp is dissolved and strained, then reduced with palm sugar into a glossy brown syrup and finished off heat with fish sauce, fried garlic, and chili. Thicker and deeper than lime-based nuoc cham, with a fruity, rounded sourness that clings to shellfish.

item.title: Tuong ot (Vietnamese chili-garlic sauce, Chin-su style)
item.description: The smooth, glossy, sweet-hot chili-garlic sauce that sits in a squeeze bottle on every pho and banh mi counter in Vietnam, best known by the Chin-su brand. Fresh red chilies and a heavy garlic load are simmered in a light sugar-vinegar brine, blended, sieved, and set with a small tapioca slurry into a pourable, cling-to-the-spoon sauce. Sweeter, brighter, and more garlic-forward than Thai-style sriracha, with no fermentation and no tomato.

item.title: Cod and crisp potatoes in rosemary-anchovy cream
item.description: A one-skillet cod and potato bake. The cream sauce is built on dissolved anchovy and a white wine reduction, so it carries glutamate and acid before any cream goes in. The potatoes are parboiled in alkaline water and roasted hard so their crust sits above the sauce line, and fried capers with toasted panko replace the soft garnish of the original.

item.title: Chili
item.description: Seven chilis that work in different ways: a whole-chile Texas bowl of red, a chili-cut beef and bean pot, New Mexico red chile pork, a tomatillo pork braise, a white chicken chili, a spiced Cincinnati meat sauce, and a vegan black bean chili.

item.title: Dried Mexican chiles
item.description: Whole dried pods of Capsicum annuum sold under names that differ from the fresh chile: ancho, mulato, guajillo, pasilla, chipotle, árbol, New Mexico, California. Most are bought for body, color, and dried-fruit flavor rather than heat, and they are the base of moles, adobos, red chile sauces, pozole, and chili.

item.title: Black bean and sweet potato chili
item.description: Black beans simmered in a purée of toasted ancho and chipotle, built on cremini mushrooms cooked until they brown and stick, which gives the pot the savory depth that meat would. Sweet potato is roasted separately so it caramelizes and keeps its shape instead of dissolving.

item.title: Black beans from dried
item.description: Dried black beans brine-soaked overnight, then simmered gently with onion, garlic, bay, and a strip of kombu until creamy inside, in a dark, seasoned bean liquid that is half the point. The base pot of beans for Mexican, Cuban, and Brazilian cooking.

item.title: Carne adovada
item.description: Pork shoulder marinated overnight in a sauce made from one chile, the dried New Mexico red pod, then baked covered for 3 hours until it falls apart in a thick, brick-red sauce. Earthy and clean rather than smoky or heavily spiced: almost no cumin, no tomato, and a little vinegar and honey to balance the chile.

item.title: Chile verde con puerco
item.description: Pork shoulder seared in lard and braised in a salsa of broiled tomatillos, poblano, Anaheim, and jalapeño chiles. The tomatillos supply both the acid and the body; charring them first trades their raw sourness for a sweeter, smoky depth.

item.title: Chunky beef and bean chili
item.description: Store-bought chili-cut beef, salted ahead and browned in bacon fat, braised with a purée of toasted ancho, guajillo, and chipotle in adobo, then finished with kidney beans and a masa-thickened gravy. A shorter braise than a whole-chuck chili because the pieces are small, and a lid on the pot because chili-cut packs often include leaner round.

item.title: Cincinnati chili
item.description: Ground beef broken into cold water rather than browned, so it cooks into a fine, saucy texture, then simmered for hours with ancho, cinnamon, allspice, cloves, cumin, and cocoa. Served over spaghetti under a heap of finely shredded cheddar, in the Greek-Macedonian tradition of Cincinnati chili parlors.

item.title: Kidney beans from dried
item.description: Dark red kidney beans brine-soaked overnight, boiled hard for 10 minutes to destroy their natural toxin, then held at a bare simmer with onion, garlic, bay, and kombu until creamy inside with intact skins. The same method works for pinto beans.

item.title: Mexican crema
item.description: Heavy cream cultured with a spoonful of buttermilk at room temperature until it thickens to a pourable, lightly sour cream, then finished with salt and lime. Higher in fat than sour cream, so it does not curdle on hot stews or salsa.

item.title: Pot of creamy white beans
item.description: Dried cannellini brine-soaked overnight, boiled 10 minutes, then cooked at a bare tremor with onion, garlic, a Parmesan rind, and olive oil until the beans are custardy and the liquid thickens into a light cream. The base for bean-and-greens braises, soups, white chili, and purées.

item.title: White chicken chili
item.description: Browned chicken thighs simmered in stock with broiled poblano, Anaheim, and jalapeño chiles and creamy white beans, then shredded. Mashed beans and a spoonful of crema give the broth body without flour, and lime keeps it bright. Turkey works the same way.

item.title: Braising
item.description: Cook collagen-rich meat or dense vegetables partly submerged in liquid, covered, below a boil for hours, until connective tissue converts to gelatin and the liquid becomes the sauce.

item.title: Bulk fermentation
item.description: The first rise of a bread dough as one mass, during which yeast produces gas and flavor while gluten develops through rest and folding; it sets most of a loaf's structure and taste.

item.title: Grilling
item.description: Cook over or under intense radiant heat from fire, coals, or a broiler element, so the surface browns and chars quickly while fat drips away and smoke adds flavor.

item.title: Poaching
item.description: Cook delicate food submerged in liquid held well below a simmer, about 70 to 85 °C, so proteins set gently and stay moist and tender instead of tightening.

item.title: Reduction
item.description: Simmer a liquid uncovered so water evaporates, concentrating flavor and thickening it through dissolved gelatin, sugars, and starches, until it reaches the body a sauce needs.

item.title: Shallow frying
item.description: Fry food in a layer of oil that comes partway up its sides, turning it once, to get a deep, even crust on each face without the volume of oil that deep-frying needs.
